qs.q: Which of the following describes the inheritance pattern and genetic basis of neurofibromatosis type 1?
o: Autosomal recessive with a defect on chromosome 22
Autosomal dominant with loss-of-function NF1 mutations
X-linked dominant disorder with mutations in merlin
qs.e: NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene located on chromosome 17q11.2. Chromosome 22 and the merlin gene are instead associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

qs.q: What is the primary inheritance pattern and characteristic hormonal profile of familial glucocorticoid deficiency?
o: X-linked recessive with normal ACTH and low aldosterone
Autosomal dominant with low ACTH and high cortisol levels
Autosomal recessive with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency
Mitochondrial inheritance with combined mineralocorticoid loss
qs.e: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder featuring isolated deficiency of glucocorticoids, elevated ACTH, and generally normal aldosterone. It leads to hypoglycemia, seizures, and increased pigmentation.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension undergoes a routine echocardiogram which shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myofiber disarray. During the physical examination, a harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, which intensifies when the patient performs the Valsalva maneuver. What is the underlying genetic inheritance pattern of this condition?
qs.e: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an autosomal dominant condition typically caused by mutations in the beta-myosin heavy chain gene. It is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

qs.q: What is the typical inheritance pattern of hereditary spherocytosis, and what percentage of patients lack a family history?
qs.e: HS is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait, but 25% of patients have no previous family history due to recessive inheritance or de novo mutations. It is not typically X-linked or autosomal recessive in the majority of cases.

qs.q: A clinical geneticist evaluates a family where multiple generations are affected by Marfan syndrome. Which of the following best characterizes the inheritance pattern and protein class involved in this condition?
o: Autosomal dominant inheritance affecting structural proteins
Autosomal recessive inheritance affecting intracellular enzymes
X-linked recessive inheritance affecting transport proteins
Multigenic inheritance involving environmental triggers exclusively
qs.e: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by defects in fibrillin-1, which is a structural protein. Autosomal dominant conditions require only one abnormal copy of the gene to manifest disease.

qs.q: Which key feature distinguishes autosomal dominant inheritance from autosomal recessive inheritance patterns?
o: Skipping of generations is commonly observed in kindreds
Vertical transmission with an affected parent in each generation
Only male offspring are clinically affected by the condition
Both parents must carry the mutant allele to express disease
qs.e: Autosomal dominant conditions classically show vertical transmission with an affected individual in nearly every generation. Recessive conditions typically skip generations and require both parents to contribute a mutant allele.

qs.q: What is the typical inheritance pattern of most cases of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
qs.e: Most cases of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are inherited as an autosomal-dominant trait. Spontaneous mutations may also account for some cases.

qs.q: Which inheritance pattern is characteristic of hereditary hemochromatosis?
qs.e: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by increased intestinal iron absorption. Autosomal dominant transmission is incorrect as the condition requires homozygosity for clinical manifestation.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Inheritance patterns describe how genetic variants are transmitted across generations and shape disease risk. Recognizing dominant, recessive, X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance guides history taking, testing and counseling.

sections.p: Genes are passed from parents to offspring in predictable ways. Patterns determine who may be affected, carrier status, and recurrence risk for families.
b: Autosomal dominant: one mutant allele causes disease; vertical transmission.
Autosomal recessive: two mutant alleles required; often seen in siblings.
X-linked dominant/recessive: sex chromosome location influences risk.

sections.p: Each cell contains two copies of autosomal genes (one from each parent) and one or two sex‑chromosome copies. Mutations can be loss‑of‑function or gain‑of‑function, affecting protein activity.
b: Dominant mutations act even when a normal allele is present.
Recessive mutations need both alleles altered to manifest.
X‑linked genes escape inactivation in females, causing variable expression.

sections.p: Pathogenic variants disrupt normal protein function, leading to disease phenotypes that follow the inheritance rule of the mutated gene.
b: Huntington disease – autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion.
Cystic fibrosis – autosomal recessive CFTR loss‑of‑function.
Hemophilia A – X‑linked recessive factor VIII deficiency.
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy – mitochondrial DNA mutation.

sections.p: Understanding inheritance guides risk assessment, genetic testing, and family counseling, especially in low‑resource settings where targeted testing may be limited.
b: Take a three‑generation pedigree to spot dominant vs recessive patterns.
Identify carriers in consanguineous families to prevent recessive disease.
Consider mitochondrial disease when only maternal relatives are affected.

t.b: What pattern of transmission is present? Helps classify the disorder and estimate recurrence risk.
Does the patient carry the pathogenic variant? Positive result confirms diagnosis; negative may need broader panel.
Is a mtDNA mutation present? Positive supports mitochondrial disease; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and maternal history.

sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, key examples, and counseling points.
b: Dominant: vertical transmission, 50% risk to offspring.
Recessive: siblings affected, 25% risk to each child of carrier couple.
X‑linked recessive: males affected, carrier females 50% risk of sons being affected.

faq.q: How can I differentiate autosomal dominant from autosomal recessive on a pedigree?
faq.a: Dominant shows affected individuals in each generation; recessive often has unaffected parents with affected siblings.

faq.q: Why do mitochondrial diseases affect only children of affected mothers?
faq.a: Mitochondria are inherited solely from the oocyte; paternal mitochondria are discarded after fertilization.

faq.q: Can a carrier of an autosomal recessive disease ever show symptoms?
faq.a: Rarely, if the mutation has a mild dominant effect or if there is a second hit (e.g., environmental stress).
